Test longer(0, 8)(5, 5)

Two AI firms choose simultaneously in this hypothetical launch game. For A, which action is strictly dominant?

options.html: Test longer, because 5 is larger than 2.
Launch now: 2 > 0 if B launches, and 8 > 5 if B tests longer.
Neither action, because launch games never have dominance.
Choose whatever gives B the highest payoff.

answerHtml: Hold B’s action fixed in each column. Launch now gives A 2 instead of 0 against launch, and 8 instead of 5 against testing. It is strictly dominant. Comparing 5 with 2 alone changes the opponent’s action and is not a dominance test. The payoffs are hypothetical profits, not evidence about actual AI firms.
sourceNote: Original application for this named topic. The lecture case’s story and payoffs have not been verified.

title: AI launch: stable does not mean best
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BLaunch nowTest longer
Launch now(2, 2)(8, 0)
Test longer(0, 8)(5, 5)

Using the hypothetical AI launch game, which statement is correct?

options.html: Both testing longer is Nash because both prefer 5 to 2.
Both launching is impossible because their joint payoff is lower.
The firms must choose the action called safer, whatever the payoffs.
Both launch now is the unique Nash equilibrium, although both prefer mutual testing.

answerHtml: Launch now strictly dominates for both firms, so both launch and receive (2, 2). At mutual testing, either firm can gain by launching alone and earning 8 rather than 5. This is the prisoners’ dilemma structure: individually stable play can be worse for both than another joint outcome.
sourceNote: Original application for this named topic. The lecture case’s story and payoffs have not been verified.

title: Price wars and a long relationship
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BHigh priceLow price
High price(9, 9)(1, 12)
Low price(12, 1)(3, 3)

This price game repeats indefinitely with perfect monitoring. A deviation from High triggers mutual Low forever from next period. With δ = 1/2, is choosing High sustainable under this grim-trigger strategy?

options.html: Yes: cooperation is worth 18; deviating now and then being punished is worth 15.
No: only the immediate 12 versus 9 matters.
No: credible future punishment can never affect today’s incentive.
Yes, because repetition guarantees cooperation for every discount factor.

answerHtml: Cooperation gives 9/(1 − 1/2) = 18. A deviation gives 12 + (1/2)3/(1 − 1/2) = 15. The threat of mutual Low is credible because Low is each firm’s stage-game best response to Low. Cooperation is sustainable under these strategies, not guaranteed as the unique outcome.

title: Escaping the price-war dilemma
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BHigh priceLow price
High price(9, 9)(1, 12)
Low price(12, 1)(3, 3)

In the displayed one-shot game, suppose a hypothetical enforceable bond makes a firm lose 4 whenever it chooses Low. If the other firm chooses High, does choosing Low remain privately profitable?

options.html: Yes: its net deviation payoff remains 12.
Yes: a bond cannot change payoffs.
No: Low now gives 12 − 4 = 8, below High’s 9.
No: any announcement is automatically binding.

answerHtml: With the other firm fixed at High, the bond reduces the deviation payoff from 12 to 8; staying High gives 9. The enforceable penalty changes the incentive comparison. Cheap talk alone would not do this.

title: Analyze a game without dominance
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BLeftRight
Up(6, 4)(0, 0)
Down(0, 0)(3, 5)

Neither player has a dominant action in this coordination game. How should you find the pure Nash equilibria?

options.html: Stop, because Nash equilibrium requires dominance.
Mark each player’s best responses and identify the cells marked for both.
Choose the single largest number anywhere in the table.
Compare A’s payoff with B’s payoff within each cell.

answerHtml: Best responses can depend on the opponent’s action even when no action is dominant. Here (Up, Left) and (Down, Right) are mutual-best-response cells. Both are pure Nash equilibria. Dominance is a useful shortcut when it exists, not a prerequisite for analysis.

title: Whose payoff are you comparing?
stemHtml: A maximizes its own profit. In one fixed column, Up gives (4, 10) and Down gives (2, 1). A’s best response is:

options.html: Down, because it reduces B’s profit.
Either, because 4 is less than B’s 10.
Down, because the two payoffs are closer.
Up, because A receives 4 rather than 2.

answerHtml: A compares its own first-number payoffs while holding the opponent’s action fixed: 4 is better than 2. A’s payoff being smaller than B’s does not itself establish a mistake. Relative profit matters only if the stated objective makes it relevant.

title: Read and solve the game tree
stemHtml:
A moves first; B observes A’s action. Terminal payoffs are (A, B).

Read the tree as text
Left, Up → (3, 6)
Left, Down → (8, 2)
Right, Up → (5, 1)
Right, Down → (1, 4)

What is B’s complete best-response plan, and what outcome does A induce?

options.html: B: Up after Left, Down after Right; A chooses Left, yielding (3, 6).
B: Down after Left, Up after Right; A chooses Left, yielding (8, 2).
B: Up after both actions; A chooses Right, yielding (5, 1).
A chooses the leaf (8, 2) directly, regardless of B.

answerHtml: After Left, B chooses Up because 6 > 2. After Right, B chooses Down because 4 > 1. A then compares the induced payoffs 3 from Left and 1 from Right and chooses Left. A strategy specifies actions at both B nodes, including the one not reached.

title: First-mover advantage through commitment
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BLeftRight
Up(6, 4)(0, 0)
Down(0, 0)(3, 5)

Now make the choices sequential and observable. A commits to its row when A moves first; B commits to its column when B moves first. What is A’s payoff when it moves first versus when B moves first?

options.html: 6 when A moves first; 3 when B moves first.
3 when A moves first; 6 when B moves first.
6 regardless of move order.
0 whenever choices are sequential.

answerHtml: If A commits first, Up induces Left and gives A 6; Down induces Right and gives A 3. A chooses Up. If B commits first, Left induces Up and gives B 4; Right induces Down and gives B 5, so B chooses Right and A receives 3. A benefits from moving first in this particular commitment game.

title: A genuine second-mover advantage
stemHtml: A commits to Left or Right. B observes and chooses Left or Right. B earns 1 if the choices differ and 0 if they match. What can B guarantee by moving second?

options.html: 0, because the first mover always has the advantage.
1, by choosing the opposite of A’s observed action.
1 only if B also has a dominant action in the simultaneous version.
A payoff determined by an unobservable action.

answerHtml: B can condition on A’s committed action: choose Right after Left and Left after Right. That guarantees B’s preferred mismatch and payoff 1. Observation creates a second-mover advantage in this game; it does not establish that moving second is best in every game.

title: The hold-up problem: before investing
stemHtml: An investor must spend 4 on an asset valuable only with one partner. Without a protective agreement, the anticipated later bargain gives the investor a gross return of 3 and its partner 7. No investment gives both 0. What does the investor choose beforehand?

options.html: Invest, because gross joint value 10 exceeds cost 4.
Invest, because the cost can be ignored before it is incurred.
Do not invest because all specific investments are socially wasteful.
Do not invest: its anticipated private net payoff is 3 − 4 = −1.

answerHtml: The investment creates positive joint surplus, 10 − 4 = 6, but the investor captures only 3 before subtracting its cost of 4. Anticipating a loss, it declines to invest. This is the hold-up incentive problem: ex post bargaining can discourage an efficient relationship-specific investment ex ante.

title: Preventing hold-up
stemHtml: In the investment example with cost 4, a credible enforceable agreement made before investing guarantees the investor a gross return of 5 if it invests. All other relevant terms are unchanged. What happens to its private incentive?

options.html: It now invests because its net return is 5 − 4 = 1 rather than −1.
Nothing changes, because all contracts are mere announcements.
It must still reject because its partner receives some surplus.
The investment cost becomes zero.

answerHtml: The agreement protects enough of the return for investment to be privately worthwhile: 5 − 4 = 1 > 0. Enforcement and timing matter. A promise that can be renegotiated away after the cost is sunk may not protect the investor’s incentive.

title: Underdog strikes back: choose the contest
stemHtml:
A small entrant chooses Out, Niche entry, or Head-on entry. After entry, the giant chooses Fight or Accommodate. Payoffs are (entrant, giant).

Out → (0, 8)
Niche, Fight → (−1, 1)
Niche, Accommodate → (3, 6)
Head-on, Fight → (−4, 4)
Head-on, Accommodate → (6, 2)

What is the backward-induction outcome in this hypothetical entry game?

options.html: Head-on entry, Accommodate, because 6 is the entrant’s largest possible payoff.
Out, because the opponent is larger.
Niche entry, Accommodate, yielding (3, 6).
Niche entry, Fight, yielding (−1, 1).

answerHtml: The giant accommodates niche entry because 6 > 1, but fights head-on entry because 4 > 2. The entrant anticipates 3 from the niche, −4 from head-on entry, and 0 from staying out. It chooses the niche. Changing the contest changes the rival’s incentives; small size alone does not determine the outcome.
sourceNote: Original application for this named topic. The lecture case’s story and payoffs have not been verified.

title: Taking on a giant: test the threat
stemHtml:
A small firm chooses Out or Enter. After entry, the giant chooses Fight or Accommodate. Payoffs are (small firm, giant).

Out → (0, 9)
Enter, Fight → (−3, 1)
Enter, Accommodate → (2, 5)

The giant announces it will fight any entrant. What is the credible outcome under the stated complete-information payoffs?

options.html: Out, because the giant’s preferred outcome is no entry.
Enter, Accommodate, because the giant prefers 5 to 1 after entry.
Enter, Fight, because announcements are irrevocable.
Out, because the small firm receives less than the giant in every positive-profit outcome.

answerHtml: After entry, accommodating gives the giant 5 rather than 1. Anticipating accommodation, the small firm earns 2 by entering rather than 0 by staying out. The no-entry payoff of 9 cannot be chosen after entry has already occurred. The hypothetical giant’s size does not make an unprofitable response credible.
sourceNote: Original application for this named topic. The lecture case’s story and payoffs have not been verified.

title: Long-term incentives
stemHtml: Why can an indefinite relationship support cooperation in some prisoners’ dilemmas when a one-shot interaction cannot?

options.html: A current deviation can sacrifice valuable future cooperation when detection and credible punishment are available.
Players must become altruistic after exactly two rounds.
An indefinite game has no current payoffs.
A threat never needs to be credible if it concerns the future.

answerHtml: The incentive comparison includes the immediate gain from deviation and its future consequences. Sufficiently valuable future cooperation can make deviation unattractive when it is detected and the continuation punishment is credible. Defection may remain an equilibrium; the future does not guarantee cooperation.

title: Optimal given the other player
stemHtml: Which condition defines a Nash equilibrium?

options.html: The sum of all payoffs is as large as possible.
Every player receives the same payoff.
Every player’s action is strictly dominant.
No player can improve its payoff by changing its own strategy alone while others keep theirs fixed.

answerHtml: Nash equilibrium is mutual best response. It does not require dominance, equality, or maximum joint welfare. This is why stable outcomes in price wars and prisoners’ dilemmas can be jointly inferior to other feasible outcomes.

title: Market failure: private and social output
stemHtml:
A competitive market has demand P = 100 − Q, MPC = 20 + Q, and constant marginal external damage of 20. There are no external benefits.

  1. Find unregulated output and explain the private condition used.
  2. Find efficient output using marginal social cost.
  3. Find a per-unit corrective tax that implements efficient output.
  4. Calculate the deadweight loss from the unregulated output and explain why efficient pollution need not be zero.
answerHtml:
Private: 100 − Q = 20 + Q → Qmarket = 40
Social: MSC = MPC + damage = 40 + Q
Efficient: 100 − Q = 40 + Q → Qefficient = 30
Corrective tax = marginal external damage at Qefficient = 20
DWL = ½ × (40 − 30) × 20 = 100

Units from 30 to 40 impose social marginal costs above their marginal benefits. The tax makes decision makers account for the omitted damage and removes this overproduction in the competitive model. Efficient output can remain positive because some production benefits exceed the full social cost; zero pollution is not the general efficiency rule.

Self-check: private output 2 practice points, social cost/output 3, tax 2, DWL and interpretation 3. Not official marks.
checks: Found private output 40 using demand = MPC.
Constructed MSC = 40 + Q and found efficient output 30.
Set the corrective tax to 20, not to the quantity or total damage.
Calculated DWL = 100 and explained the efficient pollution tradeoff.

title: Hold-up: before and after the investment
stemHtml:
A supplier can invest 6 in specialized equipment. It creates gross relationship value 14 and has no alternative-use value. The anticipated subsequent bargain allocates 4 of the gross return to the investor and 10 to its partner. Without investment, both receive 0. After investment, rejecting trade gives no gross return and cannot recover the 6.

  1. Calculate the investor’s anticipated private return and the relationship’s total net surplus. Does investment occur?
  2. Suppose the investment has nevertheless already occurred. Should the investor accept the gross return of 4 or reject trade?
  3. Explain the distinction between the decision before investment and the decision after the cost is sunk.
  4. A credible agreement signed beforehand guarantees the investor gross return 7. Does that restore its incentive to invest?
answerHtml:
Before investment, the investor anticipates 4 − 6 = −2 and does not invest. Total net surplus would be 14 − 6 = 8, so the lost investment is inefficient under the stated alternatives.

After the 6 is sunk, accepting trade gives net payoff 4 − 6 = −2, while rejecting gives 0 − 6 = −6. Accepting is better by 4. Ignoring a sunk cost for the continuation decision does not mean ignoring an avoidable cost before undertaking the project.

An enforceable prior agreement protecting gross return 7 gives the investor 7 − 6 = 1 > 0, restoring its incentive. The mechanism must actually protect the return after investment, rather than being a revocable promise.

Self-check: ex ante private and social returns 3 points, ex post comparison 3, timing explanation 2, prior agreement 2. Practice allocation only.
checks: Computed private net return −2 and social net surplus 8.
Explained why the investor accepts 4 after investing: −2 is better than −6.
Distinguished ex ante investment cost from ex post sunk cost.
Found protected net return 1 and stated why credible enforcement matters.

title: Identify a negative externality
stemHtml: Which situation is a negative externality in production?

options.html: A firm pays wages for the labour it hires.
A buyer chooses a cheaper competing product.
A factory’s emissions damage neighbours who are not compensated in the transaction.
A firm pays more for its own electricity bill.

answerHtml: The uncompensated harm falls on people outside the production transaction, so private production costs omit part of the social cost. Wages and electricity bills paid by the firm are already private costs. A competitive price effect alone is not the pollution-type external cost being modeled here.

title: Build social marginal cost
stemHtml: MPC = 10 + 2Q and marginal external damage = Q. What is MSC?

options.html: Q

answerHtml: MSC = MPC + marginal external damage = (10 + 2Q) + Q = 10 + 3Q. Do not discard private costs or add them twice.

title: Damage grows with output
stemHtml: A competitive market has demand P = 90 − Q, MPC = 10 + Q, and marginal external damage = Q. Which quantities are correct?

options.html: Unregulated Q = 80/3; efficient Q = 40.
Both quantities are 40.
Unregulated Q = 40; efficient Q = 20.
Unregulated Q = 40; efficient Q = 80/3.

answerHtml: Private equilibrium solves 90 − Q = 10 + Q, giving 40. Social marginal cost is 10 + 2Q, so efficiency requires 90 − Q = 10 + 2Q, giving 80/3 ≈ 26.67. Output-dependent damage must be included in the social curve.

title: Evaluate damage at the right output
stemHtml: Demand is P = 90 − Q, MPC = 10 + Q, and marginal external damage = Q. Efficient output is 80/3. What constant per-unit corrective tax implements it in the standard competitive model?

options.html: 40, the external damage at unregulated output.
80/3, the marginal external damage at efficient output.
80, the total output gap multiplied by 6.
0, because the damage is not constant.

answerHtml: Evaluate marginal external damage at the desired efficient quantity: t = 80/3. With this tax, private equilibrium satisfies 90 − Q = 10 + Q + 80/3, giving Q = 80/3. The efficient constant tax need not equal damage at the original unregulated quantity.

title: Private bargaining and externalities
stemHtml: Which conditions most directly support a Coase-style efficient bargain over an externality?

options.html: Unclear rights and prohibitively costly bargaining.
A guarantee that pollution is reduced to zero.
Clearly assigned rights and sufficiently low barriers and transaction costs to bargaining.
A requirement that the harmed party always owns the rights.

answerHtml: Clear rights and sufficiently low transaction costs allow the parties to compare gains and losses and bargain toward an efficient outcome under the standard assumptions. Initial rights affect transfers and wealth. They do not have to be assigned to one particular side for the basic efficiency argument.

title: Allocate pollution abatement efficiently
stemHtml: A regulator requires two units of total abatement. Firm A’s first and second abatement units cost 2 and 4; B’s first and second cost 8 and 10. There are no other effects. Which allocation minimizes total abatement cost?

options.html: A abates both units, at total cost 6.
Each firm abates one unit, at total cost 10.
B abates both units, at total cost 18.
Any allocation costs the same.

answerHtml: Choose the two cheapest available marginal abatement units: A’s first costs 2 and its second 4. Total cost is 6. A uniform one-unit requirement for each costs 2 + 8 = 10. Trading or another flexible allocation mechanism can reduce compliance cost for the same total abatement target.

title: Adverse selection or moral hazard?
stemHtml: Which is the clearest adverse-selection example?

options.html: An insured driver takes less care after coverage begins.
An employee reduces unobserved effort after receiving a fixed salary.
A factory produces emissions that harm neighbours.
People who privately know they are high-risk are more likely to buy a common-price insurance policy.

answerHtml: Adverse selection concerns hidden types affecting participation or trade. Here privately known risk influences who buys insurance. Changes in care or effort after an arrangement are moral-hazard examples, while emissions illustrate an externality.

title: Hidden action under a contract
stemHtml: After purchasing insurance, a person takes less costly care because some accident costs are borne by the insurer. The action is difficult to observe. This primarily illustrates:

options.html: Adverse selection about a fixed type before trade.
Moral hazard from changed incentives over hidden actions.
Perfect information.
A proof that all insurance is inefficient.

answerHtml: Moral hazard concerns behaviour or effort that changes under a contract when its costs are partly shifted to someone else and actions are difficult to observe. It is distinct from hidden pre-existing risk types selecting into a policy.

title: Monopoly with rising marginal cost
stemHtml: Demand is P = 100 − 2Q and marginal cost is MC = 20 + Q. Assuming an interior maximum, what quantity and price maximize profit?
answerHtml: MR = 100 − 4Q. Set MR = MC: 100 − 4Q = 20 + Q, so Q = 16. Demand gives P = 100 − 2(16) = 68. The marginal-cost value 36 at this output is not the selling price.

title: Cost recovery under regulation
stemHtml: A natural monopoly’s average total cost is above marginal cost over the relevant output range. Which statement is correct?

options.html: Marginal-cost pricing always produces positive economic profit.
Average-cost pricing necessarily eliminates all deadweight loss.
Marginal-cost pricing may require a subsidy, while average-cost pricing can cover costs with a remaining output distortion.
Regulation makes fixed costs disappear.

answerHtml: Setting P = MC can leave P below ATC, producing a loss. Setting P = ATC permits cost recovery but generally leaves P above MC in this natural-monopoly setting. Covering costs and achieving the efficient output margin are different objectives.

title: A patent does not guarantee profit
stemHtml: A patented product faces weak demand. At the firm’s best positive output, price exceeds AVC but lies below ATC. Fixed costs are unavoidable in the short run. What is the appropriate interpretation?

options.html: The firm must be earning positive economic profit because it has a patent.
It should immediately choose zero output whatever its contribution margin.
Its demand curve must be horizontal.
It makes an economic loss but may operate in the short run because it covers variable cost and contributes to fixed cost.

answerHtml: P below ATC means an economic loss. P above AVC means revenue covers variable costs and contributes toward unavoidable fixed costs, so operating can reduce the loss relative to shutdown. Monopoly protection does not guarantee sufficient demand or long-run viability.

title: Compare monopoly and efficient output
stemHtml: With downward-sloping demand, positive MC, one uniform price, and no other market failure, the standard monopoly outcome typically has:

options.html: P = MC and the efficient quantity.
P > MC and output below the level where willingness to pay equals MC.
P < MC and the largest possible output.
Zero profit under every cost curve.

answerHtml: The monopolist chooses MR = MC, while demand price exceeds MR at positive output. Thus P > MC at its chosen quantity, leaving beneficial trades unserved. Efficient output would instead equate willingness to pay with marginal social cost, equal to MC under these assumptions.

title: Customer-group pricing after fixed cost
stemHtml: Separated demands are PA = 100 − QA and PB = 60 − QB. Common MC = 20 and fixed cost = 200. At the optimum with both markets served, what is total economic profit?
answerHtml: MRA = 100 − 2QA = 20 gives QA = 40, PA = 60. MRB = 60 − 2QB = 20 gives QB = 20, PB = 40. Contribution is 40(60 − 20) + 20(40 − 20) = 2,000. Subtract fixed cost 200 to obtain profit 1,800.

title: A profitable resale route
stemHtml: A product sells to group A for 10 and group B for 20. An A buyer can resell to B for 18, incurring resale cost 3. Why does this threaten customization?

options.html: The reseller earns 18 − 10 − 3 = 5, creating an incentive to bypass the high-price channel.
The reseller necessarily loses 5.
The seller’s production MC must equal 18.
A customer’s group label guarantees resale is impossible.

answerHtml: The reseller makes 5 and the high-price buyer pays 18 instead of 20. Both have an incentive to use that route, undermining the original price separation. The practical ability to restrict arbitrage matters in addition to observing group identity.

title: Two groups, common marginal cost
stemHtml: At optimal prices, group A has |ε| = 2 and B has |ε| = 5. Both have MC = 40. Which prices follow from the interior markup rule?
answerHtml: PA = 40/(1 − 1/2) = 80. PB = 40/(1 − 1/5) = 50. A has less elastic demand and receives the higher markup and price at the respective optima.

title: AI launch without dominant strategies
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BOpen modelClosed model
Open model(4, 4)(1, 3)
Closed model(3, 1)(2, 2)

In this hypothetical simultaneous model-strategy game, which outcomes are pure Nash equilibria?

options.html: Only both Open.
Only both Closed.
Both (Open, Open) and (Closed, Closed); neither firm has a dominant action.
There is no Nash equilibrium because neither action is dominant.

answerHtml: Against Open, a firm prefers Open: 4 > 3. Against Closed, it prefers Closed: 2 > 1. Thus both matching cells are Nash, and best responses depend on the other’s action. A lacks a dominant action but can still analyze mutual best responses. These are hypothetical payoffs, not observed AI-industry outcomes.

title: AI launch as an observable sequence
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BSpecialistGeneralist
Specialist(2, 2)(5, 6)
Generalist(6, 5)(1, 1)

Use these hypothetical payoffs, but A commits to its model position first and B observes before choosing. What does backward induction predict?

options.html: A Generalist, B Specialist, giving (6, 5).
A Specialist, B Specialist, giving (2, 2).
Both Generalist, giving (1, 1).
A Specialist, B Generalist, because A cannot anticipate B.

answerHtml:
If A chooses Specialist, B prefers Generalist: 6 > 2, giving A 5. If A chooses Generalist, B prefers Specialist: 5 > 1, giving A 6. A therefore chooses Generalist and induces B’s Specialist response. Information and commitment change the decision problem.

By symmetry, if B committed first, B would choose Generalist and induce A to choose Specialist, giving A 5. A therefore earns 6 when moving first versus 5 when moving second in this hypothetical game.

title: What creates hold-up risk?
stemHtml: Which setting most directly creates the standard hold-up concern?

options.html: An investment can be fully recovered in another use and every future term is enforceably fixed.
A sunk relationship-specific investment is made before terms that determine its return are renegotiated.
A firm faces a high cost but automatically captures every benefit it creates.
Every party has perfect contractual protection of its return.

answerHtml: Specificity and incomplete protection can leave the investor dependent on its partner once investment is sunk. Anticipated renegotiation may allow the partner to capture part of the return and reduce the investor’s ex ante incentive. A high cost alone is not the hold-up mechanism.

title: Hold-up need not stop every investment
stemHtml: A specific investment costs 5 and creates gross joint value 18. The anticipated bargain gives the investor gross return 6. No investment gives it 0. What is its private choice?

options.html: Never invest, because all specific investments are blocked by hold-up.
Invest because joint value 18 is the investor’s own payoff.
Do not invest because gross return is positive.
Invest: its private net return is 6 − 5 = 1, though bargaining limits what it captures.

answerHtml: The investor still earns 1, so it invests under the stated binary alternatives. Hold-up risk can reduce private returns and distort investment incentives without necessarily eliminating every project. Assess the actual private net payoff rather than applying a blanket rule.

title: Second mover uses observation
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BRedBlue
Red(0, 2)(2, 0)
Blue(2, 0)(0, 2)

Use these payoffs with A moving first and B observing. What can B guarantee?

options.html: A payoff of 0, because A chooses the first move.
A payoff of 1 only if the game is repeated.
A payoff of 2 by matching A’s observed colour.
A payoff of 2 by choosing the opposite colour.

answerHtml: B receives 2 at a matching cell. It chooses Red after Red and Blue after Blue, guaranteeing 2. In the simultaneous version B cannot condition its action on the other firm’s realized current move. The advantage here arises from observation of a committed choice.

title: Announcement versus commitment
stemHtml: A announces a strategy first, but may freely revise it after B acts and pays no cost for revision. Why may this fail to create the first-mover advantage found in an observable commitment game?

options.html: A reversible announcement does not necessarily bind A’s later incentives or actions.
Any words spoken first create an irrevocable move.
Moving first guarantees a higher payoff regardless of the game.
The announcement makes all future payoffs equal.

answerHtml: A public message and an irreversible or otherwise credible action are different. If A can revise freely, B must consider A’s later incentives rather than treating the message as a binding choice. Some games reward credible commitment; mere chronological priority is not enough.

title: Underdog strikes back: change the response
stemHtml:
A startup may install visible technology before deciding whether to enter. Without it, the giant prefers Fight after entry: its payoff is 5 from Fight versus 3 from Accommodate, and the startup loses 2 if fought. Technology costs the startup 1 in every outcome and changes the giant’s gross Fight payoff to −1, leaving gross Accommodate at 3. The startup’s gross entry payoff if accommodated is 4; staying out has gross payoff 0.

What happens when the startup can choose the technology before entry?

options.html: It should stay out because a smaller player can never affect the giant’s best response.
It installs, enters, and is accommodated, earning net payoff 3 rather than 0 without technology.
It installs but is fought because past payoffs never change.
It receives 4 without paying the technology cost.

answerHtml: Without technology the giant would fight, deterring entry and leaving the startup 0. Technology changes the giant’s continuation comparison to −1 from fighting versus 3 from accommodation. The startup can then enter and earn 4 − 1 = 3, so it installs. The advantage comes from changing incentives, not a general rule that underdogs win.
sourceNote: Original application for this named topic. The lecture case’s story and payoffs have not been verified.

title: A commitment can be too expensive
stemHtml:
A startup may install visible technology before deciding whether to enter. Without it, the giant prefers Fight after entry: its payoff is 5 from Fight versus 3 from Accommodate, and the startup loses 2 if fought. Technology costs the startup 1 in every outcome and changes the giant’s gross Fight payoff to −1, leaving gross Accommodate at 3. The startup’s gross entry payoff if accommodated is 4; staying out has gross payoff 0.

In the displayed hypothetical startup game, change only the startup’s installation cost from 1 to 5. The technology still induces the giant to accommodate. What is the startup’s best initial choice?

options.html: Install, because deterrence of a fight guarantees positive net profit.
Install and treat an avoidable upfront cost as already sunk.
Stay out only after paying for the technology.
Do not install: the induced entry payoff is 4 − 5 = −1, below the 0 available without installing.

answerHtml: Before installation, the cost is avoidable. Installing and then entering yields −1, whereas not installing leaves the no-entry payoff 0. If installation had already occurred, entering for gross return 4 would beat staying out for gross return 0; that ex post comparison does not make the original investment worthwhile.

title: Taking on a giant: find every deviation
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BHigh priceLow price
Niche(3, 5)(2, 2)
Head-on(6, 3)(-2, 4)

Here A is a small entrant and B a giant. Choices are simultaneous. Does this hypothetical matrix have a pure Nash equilibrium?

options.html: Yes, (Niche, High price), because both payoffs are positive.
Yes, (Head-on, High price), because A’s payoff is largest there.
No: each cell gives at least one player a profitable unilateral deviation.
No game involving unequal firm sizes can have an equilibrium.

answerHtml: At Niche/High, A switches to Head-on (6 > 3). At Head-on/High, B switches to Low (4 > 3). At Head-on/Low, A switches to Niche (2 > −2). At Niche/Low, B switches to High (5 > 2). No cell is a pure Nash equilibrium. This does not rule out a mixed equilibrium.
sourceNote: Original application for this named topic. The lecture case’s story and payoffs have not been verified.

title: The giant commits first
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BHigh priceLow price
Niche(3, 5)(2, 2)
Head-on(6, 3)(-2, 4)

Use the hypothetical payoffs above, but B, the giant, now commits to High or Low first and A observes before choosing Niche or Head-on. What is the backward-induction outcome?

options.html: B chooses High, then A chooses Head-on, yielding (6, 3).
B chooses Low, then A chooses Head-on, yielding (−2, 4).
B chooses Low, then A chooses Niche, because B prefers 2 to 3.
The simultaneous game’s lack of a pure equilibrium prevents sequential analysis.

answerHtml: After High, A chooses Head-on: 6 > 3, leaving B 3. After Low, A chooses Niche: 2 > −2, leaving B 2. Anticipating this, B commits to High because 3 > 2. The observable sequential game has a definite backward-induction outcome even though the simultaneous payoff matrix lacks a pure equilibrium.

title: Repeated price wars: future punishment
stemHtml: Two firms play a price-war prisoners’ dilemma indefinitely. Each earns 8 per period at mutual High, 12 from cutting alone to Low against High, and 2 per period at mutual Low punishment. Perfect monitoring and credible grim trigger apply. With δ = 1/2, which is correct?

options.html: Deviation gives 12 forever, so cooperation is impossible.
Cooperation is worth 16 and deviation followed by punishment 14, so the incentive constraint supports cooperation.
Cooperation is worth 8 and deviation 12, so future payoffs are irrelevant.
Cooperation is uniquely guaranteed by any positive discount factor.

answerHtml: Cooperating gives 8/(1 − 1/2) = 16. Deviating gives 12 + (1/2)2/(1 − 1/2) = 14. The current deviation gain is outweighed by the loss of future cooperation. The threshold is (12 − 8)/(12 − 2) = 0.4; the specified 0.5 exceeds it. Sustainability does not imply uniqueness.

title: Change the deviation payoff
stemHtml: At mutual cooperation in a hypothetical one-shot dilemma, cooperating gives 8 and deviating alone gives 12. An enforceable bond is lost upon deviation. What is the smallest whole-number bond that makes cooperation strictly preferable against a cooperating opponent?
answerHtml: Strict preference requires 8 > 12 − bond, so bond > 4. A bond of 4 produces indifference, not strict preference. The smallest whole-number amount satisfying the inequality is 5. The comparison depends on actual enforcement of the modeled penalty.

title: Find Nash without a dominant strategy
stemHtml:
A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BLeftRight
Up(4, 4)(0, 1)
Down(2, 0)(3, 3)

Which pure Nash equilibria does this simultaneous game have?

options.html: Both (Up, Left) and (Down, Right).
Only (Up, Left), because 4 is larger than 3.
None, because best responses depend on the opponent.
Only (Up, Right).

answerHtml: A prefers Up against Left (4 > 2) and Down against Right (3 > 0). B prefers Left against Up (4 > 1) and Right against Down (3 > 0). The two diagonal cells are mutual best responses, even though neither player has a dominant action.

title: Look ahead, reason backward
stemHtml:
A moves first; B observes A’s action. Terminal payoffs are (A, B).

Read the tree as text
Left, Up → (2, 1)
Left, Down → (4, 3)
Right, Up → (5, 6)
Right, Down → (1, 2)

Which contingent plan for B and resulting path are correct?

options.html: B Up after both; A chooses Left.
B Down after both; A chooses Right.
B Down after Left, Up after Right; A chooses Right, yielding (5, 6).
B Up after Left, Down after Right; A chooses Left, yielding (2, 1).

answerHtml: At the Left node, B chooses Down because 3 > 1. At the Right node, B chooses Up because 6 > 2. A anticipates payoffs 4 from Left and 5 from Right, so chooses Right. The realized path is Right/Up; the complete B strategy also specifies Down after the unrealized Left branch.

title: Dominant strategies and outcome quality
stemHtml: In a two-player finite game, both players have a strictly dominant pure strategy. Which conclusion follows?

options.html: Their strategy pair must maximize total welfare.
Both players must receive equal payoffs.
The game cannot be a prisoners’ dilemma.
The strictly dominant strategy pair is the unique Nash equilibrium, but need not be best for both jointly.

answerHtml: Each strictly dominant strategy is the unique best response to every opponent strategy, so both must use it in any Nash equilibrium. The resulting pair can still be jointly inferior to another outcome, as in a prisoners’ dilemma. Stability and joint desirability are separate criteria.

title: A second externality policy calculation
stemHtml:
A competitive market has demand P = 140 − 2Q, marginal private cost MPC = 20 + Q, and constant marginal external damage 30. There are no external benefits.

  1. Find the unregulated market quantity and transaction price.
  2. Find the efficient quantity and the willingness to pay at that output.
  3. Find the corrective per-unit tax and distinguish the consumer and producer prices after the tax.
  4. Calculate the original deadweight loss from the externality. Explain a condition needed for private bargaining to be a useful alternative.
answerHtml:
Unregulated: 140 − 2Q = 20 + Q → Q = 40; price = 60
MSC = 50 + Q
Efficient: 140 − 2Q = 50 + Q → Q = 30
Consumer willingness to pay at Q = 30: 80
Corrective tax: 30
Consumer price after tax: 80
Producer price net of tax: 50 = MPC(30)
Original DWL: ½ × (40 − 30) × 30 = 150

The tax wedge is 80 − 50 = 30, equal to marginal external damage. The private and social output conditions differ because producers initially omit damage to outsiders. Private bargaining is more promising when relevant rights are clear and transaction costs and other bargaining barriers are sufficiently low. Initial rights affect compensation; efficient activity need not be zero.

Self-check: unregulated result 2 points, social result 2, tax and two prices 3, DWL and bargaining condition 3. Practice points only.
checks: Found unregulated quantity 40 and price 60.
Constructed MSC = 50 + Q and found efficient quantity 30.
Found tax 30, consumer price 80, and producer net price 50.
Calculated DWL 150 and stated a useful bargaining condition.

title: AI launch: simultaneous versus sequential
stemHtml:
Use this original hypothetical AI model-positioning game. In the first version A and B choose simultaneously. In the second, A commits first and B observes.

A chooses a row and B a column. Payoffs are (A, B); higher is better.

A / BOpen modelClosed model
Open model(4, 4)(1, 3)
Closed model(3, 1)(2, 2)
  1. Find each firm’s best response to each possible opponent action. Does either have a dominant strategy?
  2. Identify all pure Nash equilibria in the simultaneous game.
  3. Solve the observable sequential version by backward induction. Give B’s complete contingent strategy and the realized outcome.
  4. Explain why a reversible announcement is different from the commitment assumed in the sequential version.
answerHtml:
Against Open, each firm prefers Open (4 > 3). Against Closed, each prefers Closed (2 > 1). Neither has a dominant strategy. Both (Open, Open) and (Closed, Closed) are pure Nash equilibria in the simultaneous game.

When A commits first, B chooses Open after Open and Closed after Closed. A therefore compares its induced payoff 4 from Open with 2 from Closed and chooses Open. The sequential outcome is (Open, Open), with (4, 4). B’s complete strategy states both responses, including Closed after the branch not reached.

A reversible announcement need not bind A’s later action. B must evaluate later incentives or the information conveyed rather than automatically treating words as an irrevocable move. The definite backward-induction prediction above uses the stated observation and commitment assumptions; the hypothetical payoff numbers are not a reconstruction of a lecture case.
